8:10.text: For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.

provenance.other: The verb 'wrestle' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 6:12. The preterite 'wrestled' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Genesis 30:8, 32:24 and 32:25, all of Jacob or of Rachel; 'wrestlings' occurs in exactly one, Genesis 30:8. The Book of Mormon's participle 'wrestling' occurs in no KJV verse at all.
provenance.significance: Two sources, and the reason to name both is that Alma's sentence takes something incompatible from each. Ephesians supplies the register: the KJV uses the verb 'wrestle' exactly once, of a contest waged not against flesh and blood but in the spirit against powers — and Alma 8:9-10 sets the wrestling immediately after the statement that 'Satan had got great hold upon the hearts of the people', and says Alma 'labored much IN THE SPIRIT, wrestling'. Genesis supplies the preposition: Paul's wrestling is against, Alma's is 'with God', which is Jacob's at Peniel and no one else's. So the combatant is Paul's and the opponent is Jacob's, and what results is a sentence in which a prophet grapples with God about a city held by Satan. The Jacob half then pays: four verses later an angel appears to Alma and blesses him, which is how the night at Peniel ends and not how Ephesians 6 ends.

8:10.note: 'Alma labored much in the spirit, wrestling with God in mighty prayer.' The KJV has the verb once, at Ephesians 6:12, in the spirit and against powers; it has the past tense three times, all of Jacob, and always 'with'. Alma has the tense and preposition of Genesis and the arena of Ephesians. Recorded at moderate because a single verb is carrying the link and because 'wrestling with God in prayer' had long been ordinary evangelical English by 1830 — though that idiom is itself downstream of these same verses.
8:10.whyNot: One word of verbal contact, in a phrase already naturalized in nineteenth-century revival speech. No machine candidate reached this verse and nothing else of either source is present.

8:13.text: And cast him out of the city, and stoned him: and the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man’s feet, whose name was Saul.

provenance.route: Acts 7:57-58 with the passion predictions → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Cast him out of the city' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 7:58. 'Spit upon' occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Leviticus 15:8, Matthew 27:30, Mark 10:34 and Mark 15:19 — that is, once of ritual uncleanness and three times of Jesus. 'Reviled' occurs in exactly five KJV verses, three of them of Jesus at the cross.
provenance.significance: Alma 8:13 gives four things done to the prophet in order: they withstood his words, reviled him, spit upon him, and cast him out of their city. Every one of the last three is a KJV verb of the passion, and the last is the KJV's single occurrence of its phrase, in the verse where Stephen is put outside Jerusalem to be killed. What the sequence does is place Alma in a line the reader is expected to complete: reviled and spat upon is what happens to Jesus, cast out of the city is what happens to Stephen, and the one thing Alma 8 withholds is the stoning that follows in Acts 7:58 and the death that follows in Mark 10:34. He is thrown out and walks away weighed down with sorrow. The metalepsis is in the withheld clause — the reader who recovers Acts 7:58 finds the stones and the young man named Saul, and neither arrives; Alma is instead sent back, and it is the city that will be destroyed.

8:13.note: 'They had withstood all his words, and reviled him, and spit upon him, and caused that he should be cast out of their city.' Three KJV passion verbs in sequence, closing on the KJV's only occurrence of 'cast him out of the city', which is Stephen's martyrdom. The machine ranked Daniel 3:11 here on 'that he should be cast', which is the fiery furnace and shares only the passive construction. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his passages.

8:15.text: His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.

provenance.other: 'Thou hast been faithful' occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Matthew 25:21, Matthew 25:23 and Luke 19:17. Two of the three are the parable of the talents; the third is Luke's parable of the pounds, which reads 'faithful in a very little'.
provenance.significance: Taken alone this is a four-word commendation formula and would not carry much. What carries it is that Alma 8 goes back to Matthew 25 a second time, eleven verses later and in the angel's own idiom: at 8:26 Alma blesses Amulek in the words of Matthew 25:35, the sheep who fed the hungry stranger. So the chapter opens its supernatural frame with the lord's word to the faithful servant and closes it with the Son of Man's word to the sheep — the two halves of one Matthean discourse, used at the two ends of one episode, on the two men the episode is about. Alma is the servant found faithful; Amulek is the stranger's host. That distribution is the finding, and neither half is visible without the other.

8:15.note: 'Blessed art thou, Alma; therefore lift up thy head and rejoice … for thou hast been faithful in keeping the commandments of God.' Matthew's commendation of the faithful servant, with 'in' from Luke 19:17's variant rather than Matthew's 'over'. Moderate on its own evidence; what raises it is Alma 8:26's use of Matthew 25:35 for Amulek, which makes this chapter a two-point sampling of a single chapter of Matthew. The machine proposed Luke 19:17 here, which is the same formula in the parallel parable, and the choice between them is not decidable on four words.
8:15.whyNot: Four common words in a formula the KJV itself uses three times, and the preposition Alma has is Luke's rather than Matthew's. If the Matthew 25:35 row at 8:26 were withdrawn, this row should be withdrawn with it.

8:16.text: Arise, go unto Nineveh, that great city, and preach unto it the preaching that I bid thee.

provenance.other: 'Three days' journey' occurs in exactly seven KJV verses; the one that attaches it to a city rather than to a march is Jonah 3:3, 'Nineveh was an exceeding great city of three days' journey', a KJV singleton for 'an exceeding great city'. 'The second time, saying' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Jeremiah 1:13, Jeremiah 13:3 and Jonah 3:1. Alma 8 has no phrase of Jonah verbatim, which is why this is figural and kjvSpecific is 'uncertain'.
provenance.significance: The shape is Jonah's and the tell is the measurement. Alma 8:6 has him travel 'three days' journey' and arrive at a city; the KJV's one use of that distance as the measure of a city is Nineveh's. Thereafter the sequence runs point for point: a prophet sent to a great wicked city, who leaves it — Jonah by ship, Alma cast out and 'about to set my back towards this land forever' (8:24) — and is then commissioned a second time in the same words as the first, with the destruction now named. Jonah 3:1's 'the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time' is answered at Alma 8:29, 'And the word came to Alma, saying, Go'; Jonah 3:4's 'Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown' is answered at 8:16, 'except they repent, the Lord God will destroy them.' Alma even arrives, like Jonah, sick of the errand and 'weighed down with sorrow'. The suppressed correspondence is the ending. Jonah's book exists to record that Nineveh repented and was spared, and that the prophet was angry about it. Ammonihah does not repent, and is destroyed in Alma 16. The type-scene is set up so that its one available outcome is the one Jonah did not get, and the reader who knows Jonah is told, by the shape alone and before any of it happens, that this city is being given its second chance.
provenance.alternative: Jonah 1:2's 'Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it' is the first commission and equally close; the second is preferred because Alma 8:16 is explicitly a re-sending.

8:16.note: 'I am sent to command thee that thou return to the city of Ammonihah, and preach again unto the people of the city … except they repent, the Lord God will destroy them.' No wording of Jonah is reproduced, so this is catalogued on narrative form: the prophet sent to a great city, rejected, re-commissioned in the same terms, and given a threat of destruction to deliver. What keeps it from being a bare thematic association is Alma 8:6, where the city is reached at 'three days' journey' — the KJV's measure of Nineveh, and of no other city. The machine proposed 2 Samuel 15:34 here on 'thou return to the', which is Hushai being sent back to Absalom, and has nothing else. Compare the Jonah link already made at 1 Nephi 2:13, where 'that great city' is the borrowed phrase; there the epithet is taken and here the plot is, and Alma is a different hand.

8:18.text: So he went another way, and returned not by the way that he came to Bethel.

provenance.other: 'Another way' occurs in exactly four KJV verses: 1 Kings 13:10, 1 Kings 18:6, Matthew 2:12 and James 2:25. 'Come home with me, and eat bread' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 13:15; 'did eat bread in his house' occurs in exactly one, 1 Kings 13:19. Both belong to the same episode as the first.
provenance.significance: 1 Kings 13 is the KJV's one story built entirely out of these elements: a man of God sent against a city to prophesy, forbidden to eat bread there, who leaves by 'another way'; who is then met by a local prophet saying 'Come home with me, and eat bread'; who goes back with him and 'did eat bread in his house'. Alma 8 runs the same five moves in the same order — sent against Ammonihah, hungry, entering 'by another way', met by Amulek offering food and lodging, eating bread in his house and being filled. The reversal is the whole point and it is exact. In 1 Kings the eating is the disobedience: the man of God had been charged 'Eat no bread, nor drink water, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest', and returning to eat is what a lion kills him for on the road. In Alma the eating is the obedience — he entered by another way because an angel had sent him back, and the man who feeds him is the man the angel had prepared and is about to become his fellow-witness. Where 1 Kings 13 makes hospitality the trap that destroys the prophet, Alma 8 makes it the means by which the mission is saved. That inversion is the argument for reading the borrowing as deliberate rather than accidental: an accident would not have gotten the sequence right and the moral backwards.

8:18.note: 'He returned speedily to the land of Ammonihah … and he entered the city by another way.' The verbal contact is one four-verse phrase; the case rests on sequence, and on the fact that the two KJV singletons of the same episode ('Come home with me, and eat bread'; 'did eat bread in his house') are matched by Alma 8:20-22 in order. Recorded at moderate for that reason — the wording will not carry it alone, and the register at 8:21 notes that 'bread and meat', a KJV singleton at Genesis 45:23, is not a contributor here. No machine candidate reached 8:18 at all.
8:18.whyNot: One shared phrase and a narrative shape. A prophet arriving hungry and being fed is a common enough scene in the KJV (compare 1 Kings 17:10-16, Judges 6:19) that the ordering could be coincidence; the inversion of the moral is what argues against coincidence, and inversion is not evidence a sceptic has to accept.

8:26.text: For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:

provenance.other: 'Took me in' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:35, and 'I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same. 'He was afterward an hungred' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 4:2, the only KJV verse joining fasting to subsequent hunger.
provenance.significance: Alma's sentence to Amulek reproduces two of Matthew 25:35's three clauses and its verdict: hungry and fed, taken in, therefore blessed. The one word that fixes the source is 'took me in', which the KJV uses in this sense once. What follows from recovering the context is the chapter's severest claim. Matthew 25:35 is spoken by the Son of Man on the throne of judgment to the sheep at his right hand, and it is glossed four verses later — 'Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.' So when Alma tells Amulek 'because thou hast fed me and took me in, thou art blessed', he is speaking the words of the judge about himself, and the blessing is the judge's own 'Come, ye blessed of my Father' of 25:34. The other half of the parable is what the chapter has already narrated: Ammonihah refused the hungry prophet and cast him out, which is Matthew 25:42's 'I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat.' Alma 16 destroys the city. The parable's two verdicts are distributed across one chapter and its sequel, the sheep in Amulek's house and the goats in the city outside it. Note also that Alma's reason for hunger — 'for I had fasted many days' — is Matthew 4:2's, the only KJV verse where a fast is the cause of hunger, and there the fast precedes a confrontation with Satan; Alma 8:9 had said that Satan 'had got great hold upon the hearts of the people'.

8:26.note: 'Because thou hast fed me and took me in, thou art blessed: for I was an hungered, for I had fasted many days.' Two clauses of Matthew 25:35, including its one-verse phrase 'took me in', with the parable's verdict attached; and the hunger explained in Matthew 4:2's terms. The 1830 'an hungered' modernizes the KJV's 'an hungred' but preserves the archaic construction, which no version after the KJV has. No machine candidate reached this verse or 8:19.

8:31.text: But all this was done, that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Then all the disciples forsook him, and fled.

provenance.other: 'This was done, that' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 1:22, 21:4 and 26:56 — all narratorial purpose clauses, and all Matthew's. 'Twelve legions of angels' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 26:53. 'Shew my power in thee' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 9:17.
provenance.significance: The borrowing is a whole argument, not a phrase. Matthew 26:53-56 is the KJV's one passage in which a man declares that overwhelming power is available to him, declines to use it, submits to arrest, and has a narrator explain the restraint in a purpose clause beginning 'all this was done, that'. Alma 8:31 does each of those four things in order: power such that no dungeon could hold them and no man could slay them, 'nevertheless they did not exercise their power', bound and cast into prison, 'Now this was done that the Lord might show forth his power in them.' The formula is Matthew's — three KJV verses have it and all three are his. The divergence is in what the purpose clause names, and it is the interesting part: Matthew's restraint is for the fulfilment of scripture, Alma's is for a demonstration of power, so the very capacity that was renounced is the thing the renunciation exists to display. The Pauline singleton behind that second half is Romans 9:17's 'that I might shew my power in thee', spoken of Pharaoh — of a man hardened, in a narrative of hardened hearts, which is what Alma 8:11 has just said of Ammonihah.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 1:22 and 21:4 have the same formula in the same author; 26:56 is preferred because only there is the clause explaining a deliberate non-use of power at an arrest.

8:31.note: 'They had power given unto them, insomuch that they could not be confined in dungeons … nevertheless they did not exercise their power until they were bound in bands and cast into prison. Now this was done that the Lord might show forth his power in them.' A four-word narratorial formula the KJV uses three times, all in Matthew, deployed at the one point of Alma 8 that matches its Matthean setting. The 1830 reads 'show' where the KJV would have 'shew', which is a point against KJV-specific orthography here and is recorded as such; the formula itself is unaffected. The machine did rank Matthew 26:56 at this verse, on the same run.
